The X-Files is a science fiction television series that aired on Fox from 1993 to 2018 with intermittent breaks, becoming one of the most culturally resonant and commercially successful television programs of the nineteen-nineties and two-thousands. Created by Chris Carter, the show featured two FBI agents investigating paranormal cases, blending conspiracy thriller elements, procedural investigation, romance, and an overarching mythology that kept audiences engaged across nine seasons and two theatrical films.

The show premiered on Fox in September 1993 and ran for nine seasons totaling two hundred two episodes through 2002. It was later revived for limited runs and became one of Fox's flagship programs during its development as a major network. The series starred David Duchovny as Agent Fox Mulder, a believer in the paranormal hunting the truth, and Gillian Anderson as Agent Dana Scully, a skeptical scientist whose partnership with Mulder defined the show's dynamic.

The format combined mythology episodes advancing an overarching government conspiracy narrative about extraterrestrial contact and alien government collusion, with monster of the week standalone episodes exploring paranormal phenomena. The show's chemistry between Mulder and Scully, their unresolved romantic tension, contrasting worldviews, and genuine affection, became the emotional core that sustained the series through inconsistent mythology writing. The show created a cultural obsession with conspiracy theories, government secrecy, and extraterrestrial life. It introduced the phrase the truth is out there and the image of the I Want to Believe poster became iconic.

Famous episodes include Home, a story about a family living in a depraved, isolated compound, and Bad Blood, a humorous episode told from both agents' contrasting perspectives. Mythology entries advanced the alien conspiracy narrative throughout the series. The show influenced subsequent television series in embracing serialized storytelling, mythology-driven narratives, and the appeal of romantic partnership between protagonists, influencing shows like Fringe and Supernatural.
